title: Islam (I1): Worship in the Mosque, Prayer, the Qur'an and Leaders
summary: Define, describe and explain the mosque and its features, the artefacts of prayer, the adhan, wudu, salah, Jumu'ah, du'a, dhikr, respect for the Qur'an, and the imam and mu'azzin.

sections.h: I1.1 The mosque: centre for worship and for the ummah
p: Teach the key terms and why the mosque matters.
• Mosque (masjid): means 'place of prostration'. It is a centre for Muslim worship, where Muslims pray together.
• Ummah: the worldwide community of Muslims. The mosque is the centre of the ummah in a local area.
• Besides prayer, mosques often host Qur'an classes, community events, advice, charity collections and celebrations such as Eid.
• Any clean place can be used for prayer, but the mosque brings the community together, especially on Fridays.

b: 'State what is meant by masjid.' It means 'place of prostration' and is the Muslim place of worship.
Part (c) link: 'The mosque is the most important place for a Muslim.' Views: community, prayer, learning; against: prayer can be anywhere, faith lived daily.

sections.h: I1.2 Key features of a mosque: define, describe and explain
p: Each feature has a purpose and a meaning. Practices differ in different Muslim communities.
• Minaret ('site of light'): the tower of the mosque. Traditionally the adhan was called from it. It marks the mosque.
• Dome: symbolises the vault of heaven. It also helps the sound of prayers carry.
• Qiblah: the direction of Makkah, which Muslims face to pray.
• Mihrab: a niche in the qiblah wall that shows the direction of prayer.
• Minbar: a stepped platform from which the imam gives the Friday sermon.
• Musalla (prayer hall): the main room where people pray. It is carpeted, often with lines to help people line up.

• Separate areas for men and women: many mosques have separate spaces so that people can pray without distraction and with modesty. Some mosques have a balcony or a different room for women. Views differ about how the spaces are arranged.

• Architecture and calligraphy: mosques use geometric patterns and Arabic calligraphy of Qur'an verses. There are no pictures or statues of humans or animals because Muslims believe only God should be worshipped and images could lead to idol worship.

b: Some mosques are large with domes and minarets; others are simple rooms.
Styles vary by country: Ottoman, Mughal, West African mud-brick mosques.
Features differ, but all face the qiblah.

sections.h: I1.3 Artefacts used in worship
p: Teach what each object is, how it is used and what it means.
• Copies of the Qur'an: the holy book, kept in a clean place and handled with care. Often placed on a stand (rehal).
• Compass: shows the direction of the qiblah, useful in travel or in buildings with no mihrab.
• Prayer mat (sajjadah): a clean place to pray. Often has a niche design that points to Makkah.
• Turbah (prayer stone): a small tablet of clay on which the forehead rests in prostration, used mostly by Shi'ah Muslims, because it comes from the earth.
• Misbahah (prayer beads, tasbih): used for dhikr, counting the repeated praise of God (often 33 times for each phrase).

b: Describe: a prayer mat is a rug used for prayer.
Explain: it keeps the place clean and helps Muslims focus on worship.
Different views: not all Muslims use a turbah; Sunni Muslims often pray on carpets or mats.

sections.h: I1.4 Public and private worship: adhan, wudu and salah
p: These are central to Muslim daily life.

• Adhan (call to prayer): called by the mu'azzin before each prayer. It announces the time and invites people to worship. It begins 'Allahu Akbar' (God is greatest). It is also whispered into a newborn baby's ear.
• Wudu (ablution): washing the hands, mouth, nose, face, arms, head and feet before prayer. It shows purity and readiness to meet God.
• Salah (formal prayer) and the five prayer times: Fajr (dawn), Dhuhr (midday), Asr (afternoon), Maghrib (sunset), Isha (night).

• Rak'ahs: units of prayer, a set sequence of movements: standing, bowing, prostrating and sitting, with recitation of the Qur'an and praise of God. The number of rak'ahs varies by prayer (for example Fajr has 2, Maghrib has 3, others have 4).
• Significance: the movements show humility and submission to God. Praying together builds unity.

ex.t: Order of salah in simple words
b: Intention and takbir (raising hands, 'Allahu Akbar').
Standing: reciting Surah al-Fatihah and another passage.
Bowing (ruku), standing again, prostration (sujud).
Sitting and ending with greetings of peace.

sections.h: Jumu'ah, du'a and dhikr
p: More forms of worship the syllabus names.

• Jumu'ah prayer (Friday midday prayer): the most important weekly prayer, prayed at the mosque with a sermon (khutbah). Muslim men are required to attend; women may attend. It brings the community together.
• Du'a (private prayer): personal asking and speaking to God in one's own words, often with raised hands, before or after salah, with preparation such as wudu and praising God.

• Dhikr (remembrance): repeating names or phrases of God, for example 'SubhanAllah', 'Alhamdulillah', 'Allahu Akbar', often with prayer beads. It is a devotional practice that brings calm and closeness to God.
• Different views: some Muslims, especially Sufi groups, place great weight on dhikr and use it in group gatherings. Others value it as a personal practice.

b: Public: salah and Jumu'ah with the community, led by the imam.
Private: du'a and dhikr alone or at home.
Evaluate: 'Private prayer is more important than public worship.' Give views and a judgement.

sections.h: The Qur'an in worship and respect for it
p: The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam. Muslims believe it is God's word as revealed to Prophet Muhammad (pbuh).
• Use in public worship: recited in salah, in the Friday sermon and during Ramadan.
• Use in private prayer and study: read, memorised and studied at home and in classes.
• Different views: some Muslims stress recitation in Arabic; others emphasise understanding translated meanings. Some memorise the whole Qur'an (hafiz).
• Respectful treatment: wash (wudu) before touching it, keep it clean and in a high place, never on the floor, wrap it in cloth, do not touch it with unclean hands, and do not put other items on top.

ex.t: Explain why Muslims treat the Qur'an with respect
b: It is the word of God.
It guides every part of life.
Respect shows love for God and obedience.

sections.h: I1.5 Leaders: the imam and the mu'azzin
p: Islam has no priesthood, but there are leaders in the mosque.

• Imam: a Muslim religious leader. He leads the prayers, delivers the Friday sermon, teaches the Qur'an, advises families and officiates at weddings and funerals. He is often chosen for knowledge and character.
• Mu'azzin (muezzin): the person who gives the call to prayer (adhan). Many mosques now use recordings or loudspeakers.
• In Shi'ah communities, imam can also have a special meaning for the descendants of Ali (see I2.5).
• Different views: some communities have a paid imam; in others, a respected member leads prayer.

b: Explain the role of the imam in the mosque.
He leads prayer; gives the khutbah; teaches; supports families; leads at marriage and funerals.
Link: this shows the mosque as a community centre.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes to look for.
• Confusing the imam and the mu'azzin.
• Saying the minaret is where Muslims pray, instead of where the adhan was called.
• Forgetting qiblah is the direction of Makkah.
• Writing 'Allah' as a different god from the God of other religions. Use 'God (Allah)'.
• Describing prayer without explaining meaning.
Revision tasks:
• Draw and label a mosque plan with qiblah, mihrab, minbar and musalla.
• List the five prayers with times.
• Write three sentences on respect for the Qur'an.

b: I can define 10 words from I1.
I can describe wudu and salah in order.
I can explain why there are no images in mosques.
I can write a part (c) question on public and private worship.

activity: Make a labelled mosque plan with minaret, dome, qiblah wall, mihrab, minbar and musalla. Beside it write a one-line meaning for each feature. Then write a part (b) answer on 'Explain the importance of salah for Muslims' using at least three points.

o: The direction of Makkah that Muslims face in prayer

check.q: Who gives the call to prayer?
Which prayer is Friday midday prayer?

title: Islam (I2 and I3): Beliefs, Prophet Muhammad, Sunni and Shi'ah, Hajj and Umrah
summary: Define, describe and explain the Six Articles of Faith, the five roots of Usul ad-Din, the Five Pillars, the life of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), Sunni and Shi'ah origins, the Qur'an, and the places and rites of Hajj and Umrah.

sections.h: I2.1 The Six Articles of Faith
p: These are the basic beliefs of Sunni Muslims (and shared by Shi'ah with different emphasis).
• Tawhid: the oneness of God. God is one, with no partners. The most important belief.
• Risalah: belief in prophets sent by God to guide humanity, such as Ibrahim, Musa, Isa and Muhammad (pbuh).
• Akhirah: life after death. People will be judged by God on the Day of Judgement and will go to Paradise or Hell.
• Mala'ikah: belief in angels, God's servants such as Jibril who brought revelation.
• Qadar: predestination, that God knows and has power over all things. Muslims also believe humans have free will and responsibility.
• Kutub: God's holy books, including the Torah, Psalms, Gospel and the Qur'an, the final book.
• Different views and impact: Muslims may differ on how they understand Qadar and free will. Belief in akhirah shapes honesty, prayer and care for others.

b: 'Outline the Muslim belief in tawhid.' God is one and has no partners.
Link to daily life: Muslims worship only God and avoid idol worship.
Evaluate: 'Tawhid is the most important belief in Islam.' Views and judgement.

sections.h: I2.2 The five roots of Usul ad-Din (Shi'ah)
p: This is a new topic in the 2025 to 2027 syllabus. These are the five basic beliefs in Shi'ah Islam.
• Tawhid: oneness of God.
• 'Adl: divine justice. God is always fair and just.
• Risalah (also called Nubuwwah): prophets.
• Imamah: the authority of the imams, the leaders from the family of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) chosen by God, beginning with Ali.
• Mi'ad: the Day of Resurrection, when all people are raised for judgement.
• Different views: Sunni Muslims do not hold Imamah as a root of religion. Shi'ah consider it essential.
• Impact on daily life: belief in God's justice encourages fairness; belief in the imams guides Shi'ah in religious knowledge and practice.

ex.t: Compare Six Articles and Five Roots
b: Shared: tawhid, prophets, life after death.
Different: Sunni list includes angels, holy books and qadar; the Shi'ah roots include divine justice and imamah.
Teach this carefully and without judging either group.

sections.h: I2.3 The Five Pillars of Islam
p: The Five Pillars are the main acts of worship all Muslims try to follow.
• Shahadah: the declaration of faith: 'There is no god but God and Muhammad is the messenger of God.' Saying it with sincerity makes a person Muslim.
• Salah: prayer five times a day.
• Sawm: fasting during the month of Ramadan.
• Zakah: obligatory charity, usually 2.5% of savings above a minimum amount, given to people in need.
• Hajj: pilgrimage to Makkah once in a lifetime for those who are able.
• Different views: Shi'ah Muslims also teach the Ten Practices of the religion (Furu' ad-Din), which include the five pillars with other duties.
• Impact on daily life: they give discipline, community, generosity and closeness to God.

b: 'Explain the importance of the Five Pillars for Muslims.'
Give at least three points with explanation, such as unity, discipline and obedience to God.
Add an example: fasting in Ramadan shows self-control and empathy for the poor.

sections.h: I2.4 Prophet Muhammad (pbuh)
p: Teach the life in order, with the key events and their importance.
• Early life: born in Makkah around 570 CE, orphaned young, known as al-Amin (the trustworthy) for his honesty.

• First revelation: around 610 CE, in the cave of Hira', the angel Jibril brought the first words of the Qur'an ('Read!'). Muhammad (pbuh) was frightened but was comforted by his wife Khadijah. This marks the start of prophethood.
• Persecution: when he preached the oneness of God and equality, the leaders of Makkah opposed him, because it challenged their idols, trade and power. Early Muslims were persecuted.
• Hijrah: the flight to Madinah in 622 CE. It is the start of the Islamic calendar. There he formed the first Muslim community.
• Final messenger and Seal of the Prophets: Muslims believe he is the last prophet and that the Qur'an is the final revelation.

ex.t: Why does the hijrah matter today?
b: It marks the start of the Muslim calendar.
It shows patience, faith and sacrifice.
It established the first Muslim community.

sections.h: I2.5 and I2.6 Sunni and Shi'ah origins; the Qur'an
p: Teach respectfully and factually.
• After the death of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) in 632 CE, Muslims disagreed on who should lead.
• Sunni: believe the community chose Abu Bakr as the first caliph, followed by 'Umar and 'Uthman. They respect the early caliphs.
• Shi'ah: believe the Prophet chose his cousin and son-in-law Ali as leader, and that leadership belongs to the Prophet's family. They teach the Twelve Imams, descendants of Ali.
• The Qur'an: seen as the final revelation and authority, and a source of moral principles.

• Requirements and restrictions: Surah Al-An'am 6:151–153 and Surah Al-Isra' 17:23–39 teach, for example, worship God alone, be kind to parents, do not kill unjustly, do not commit adultery, give full measure, keep promises, and care for orphans.
• Interpretation: some Muslims stress literal meaning; others use scholarship and context. All agree on the Qur'an's authority.

ex.t: Compare Sunni and Shi'ah in a short table
b: Leadership after Muhammad (pbuh): Abu Bakr and the caliphs (Sunni) | Ali and the imams (Shi'ah).
Number of imams in the main Shi'ah tradition taught here: twelve.
Both: follow the Qur'an, the Five Pillars and the Prophet's example.

sections.h: I3.1 and I3.2 Hajj: the importance and the performance
p: Hajj is the pilgrimage to Makkah. It takes place in the month of Dhu al-Hijjah.
• Goals: spiritual (forgiveness, closeness to God, equality) and physical (completing the rites).
• Challenges: heat, crowds, tiredness, cost. They test patience and faith.
• Stages and places (as in the syllabus):
• Ihram: pilgrims wear simple white clothes (men) or modest dress (women) to show equality and purity.

• Makkah and the Ka'bah: the cube-shaped building at the heart of the Sacred Mosque. Pilgrims walk around it seven times (tawaf) and walk between the hills of Safa and Marwa (sa'y), remembering Hajar's search for water for her son Isma'il.
• The well of Zamzam: the miraculous water that appeared for Hajar and Isma'il; pilgrims drink from it.
• Mina: pilgrims stay in tents and throw pebbles at pillars (stoning), recalling Ibrahim's rejection of temptation.
• 'Arafat: the most important day. Pilgrims stand on the plain praying and asking for forgiveness. Mount of Mercy (Jabal Rahmah) is a hill on the plain.
• Muzdalifah: pilgrims spend the night under the open sky and collect pebbles.

ex.t: Order of the main Hajj rites (a simple outline)
b: Enter ihram and go to Makkah for tawaf.
Travel to Mina, then 'Arafat for the day of standing.
Night at Muzdalifah, then stoning at Mina.
Sacrifice, shaving or cutting hair, final tawaf and sa'y.
End: Eid al-Adha is celebrated.

sections.h: I3.3 and I3.4 'Umrah, Makkah and Madinah
p: 'Umrah and the two cities.
• 'Umrah: the 'lesser pilgrimage'. It can be done at any time of the year.
• Similarities with Hajj: wearing ihram, tawaf around the Ka'bah and sa'y between Safa and Marwa.
• Differences: 'Umrah is shorter, is not compulsory, and does not include 'Arafat, Muzdalifah or stoning. Hajj is one of the Five Pillars.
• Makkah: birthplace of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh), where early Muslims were persecuted and from where the hijrah began.
• Madinah: destination of the hijrah; the first Muslim community was established there; the site of the first mosque; and the place where Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) died and is buried.

b: 'Hajj is more important than any other Pillar.' Evaluate.
For: only done once, tests everything, unites Muslims worldwide.
Against: shahadah is the foundation; salah is daily; not everyone can afford Hajj.
Judgement: reasoned conclusion with evidence.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Mixing up the Five Pillars with the Six Articles.
• Treating the five roots of Usul ad-Din as the same as the Five Pillars.
• Saying Hajj happens in Ramadan. It happens in Dhu al-Hijjah.
• Confusing Hajj and 'Umrah.
• Presenting Sunni and Shi'ah as unfriendly or in conflict instead of as two traditions with different history.
Revision tasks:
• Make a three-column table: Six Articles | Five Roots | Five Pillars.
• Draw a Hajj map with Makkah, Mina, Muzdalifah, 'Arafat.
• Write two evaluation points for and against the statement above.

b: I can list the Six Articles, Five Roots and Five Pillars.
I can explain the hijrah and its importance.
I can explain two differences between Sunni and Shi'ah views on leadership.
I can describe the Hajj rites in order.

activity: Make a poster that compares the Six Articles of Faith, the five roots of Usul ad-Din and the Five Pillars. Under it add a timeline of Prophet Muhammad's life with five events. Finally, write a part (c) answer plan on whether Hajj is the most important Pillar.

check.q: Which belief is the oneness of God?
Which new topic was added to the Islam content in 2025?
o: The five roots of Usul ad-Din
The flight of Prophet Muhammad (pbuh) and early Muslims from Makkah to Madinah

title: Islam (I4): Eid al-Adha, Ramadan and Eid al-Fitr
summary: Define, describe and explain 'Id al-Adha, the fast of Ramadan including iftar, suhur, i'tikaf and Laylat al-Qadr, 'Id al-Fitr, and how festivals and fasts are changing today.

sections.h: Teach each festival with one pattern
p: Use the same questions for each festival and fast.
• What is it, and when is it? (Islamic calendar is lunar, so dates move about 10 to 11 days earlier each year.)
• What does it remember?
• How is it kept (customs, food, prayer)?
• Religious reasons: origins, purpose and symbolism.
• Social significance.
• Different ways it is observed.
• Changes and different feelings today.

b: Ramadan: ninth month of the Islamic calendar.
'Id al-Fitr: the first day of Shawwal, the month after Ramadan.
'Id al-Adha: the tenth day of Dhu al-Hijjah, the month of Hajj.

sections.h: I4.1 'Id al-Adha (feast of sacrifice)
p: 'Id al-Adha is one of the two main festivals.
• It is the celebration at the end of Hajj, kept by Muslims all over the world.
• Connection to Ibrahim (AS): Muslims remember God's testing of Ibrahim, who was ready to sacrifice his son. God provided a ram instead. It shows complete trust and obedience.
• Importance of sacrifice in Muslim life: giving up something valued for God and for others.

• Customs: special 'Id prayer at the mosque or open ground, wearing best clothes, greeting 'Id Mubarak', sacrificing an animal for those who can afford it, and sharing the meat in three parts: for the family, for relatives and friends, and for the poor.
• Religious reasons: obedience, trust, sacrifice and thankfulness.
• Social significance: sharing food, visiting family, helping the poor.
• Different ways: customs vary by country, such as the type of animal and the dishes cooked; some give money to charities to buy and distribute the meat.

b: Point: 'Id al-Adha remembers Ibrahim's willingness to obey God.
Explain: this teaches trust and sacrifice.
Link: Muslims share meat with the poor to show care for the community.

sections.h: I4.2 The fast of Ramadan: rules and benefits
p: Ramadan is the month of fasting. It is one of the Five Pillars (sawm). It is the month in which the Qur'an was first revealed.
• Rules: fast from dawn to sunset. No eating, drinking, smoking or marital relations during the day. Avoid bad speech and behaviour.
• Exemptions: children, the elderly, the sick, travellers, pregnant or nursing women and women who are menstruating are not required to fast.
• Compensations: missed days are made up later, or people who cannot fast give food to a poor person (fidyah). Deliberately breaking a fast needs a larger penalty.
• Spiritual benefits: self-control, thankfulness, empathy for the poor, closeness to God and a fresh start.
• Iftar: the meal to break the fast at sunset, often beginning with dates and water, then prayer and a shared meal. Physically, it restores energy; spiritually, it shows gratitude and fellowship.
• Suhur: the pre-dawn meal. It gives strength for the day and follows the Prophet's example.
• Purpose for the individual and the ummah: personal discipline and unity, as Muslims all over the world fast together.

b: Saying everyone must fast. Exemptions exist.
Saying fasting is only about food. It includes behaviour and prayer.
Forgetting that dates vary because of the lunar calendar.

sections.h: I4.2 continued: i'tikaf, Laylat al-Qadr and giving
p: The last ten days of Ramadan are especially important.
• I'tikaf: a spiritual retreat in the mosque during the last ten days of Ramadan. Muslims spend time in prayer, Qur'an reading and remembrance, with little talk of worldly matters.

• Laylat al-Qadr (Night of Power): the night the Qur'an was first revealed. It is believed to be one of the odd nights in the last ten days, often the 27th. The Qur'an says it is better than a thousand months. Muslims pray, recite the Qur'an and ask forgiveness.
• Sadaqah: voluntary giving. Muslims give more in Ramadan, and also pay zakat al-Fitr, a small donation for the poor before the 'Id prayer. Giving shows concern and gratitude.
• Religious reasons for observing Ramadan: obedience to God, learning discipline, remembering the revelation.
• Social significance: family and community iftars, charity drives, a sense of belonging.
• Different ways: some communities have long evening prayers (tarawih); some pray at home; patterns of food and gatherings differ by country.

b: 'The most important benefit of fasting is spiritual.' Evaluate.
For: self-control, closeness to God, gratitude.
Against: the social benefits of unity and charity also matter; fasting has health aspects.
Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.

sections.h: I4.3 'Id al-Fitr (the end of Ramadan)
p: 'Id al-Fitr means 'the festival of breaking the fast'.
• It celebrates the end of Ramadan. It starts when the new moon of Shawwal is seen.

• Features: special 'Id prayers in congregation, greetings such as 'Id Mubarak, special food prepared and shared with family and friends, wearing new or best clothes, community celebrations, presents (especially for children) and charity (zakat al-Fitr).
• Religious reasons: thanking God for the strength to fast, celebrating completing Ramadan, and sharing joy with the whole community.
• Social significance: families reunite, neighbours are visited, the poor are included.
• Different ways: sweets and dishes vary around the world; some communities hold large fairs, others small gatherings.

b: 'Id al-Fitr: end of Ramadan; thanks; sweets and gifts.
'Id al-Adha: end of Hajj; sacrifice; sharing meat.
Both: special 'Id prayer, new clothes, visiting family, charity.

sections.h: I4.4 Changes to festivals and fasts
p: Teach how practice is changing and why people feel differently.

• Changes in the modern world: shift work and school times affect fasting; online iftars and Qur'an classes; moon sighting by astronomy or by eye (different communities follow different methods); commercial 'Id markets.
• Different views: some Muslims welcome changes that help people take part. Others want to keep traditional methods, for example moon sighting by eye.
• Feelings: some worry that festivals are becoming too commercial or that tradition is lost; others see change as a way to keep the faith alive.

b: 'Ramadan is too difficult to keep in the modern world.' Evaluate.
For: long hours at work or school, hot climates, health.
Against: exemptions exist, community support, deep spiritual value.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision table and common mistakes
p: Revision table:
• 'Id al-Adha | 10 Dhu al-Hijjah | Ibrahim's trust and sacrifice | animal sacrifice and sharing meat.
• Ramadan | 9th month | revelation of the Qur'an | fasting, iftar, suhur.
• Laylat al-Qadr | last ten nights | first revelation | night prayers.
• 'Id al-Fitr | 1 Shawwal | end of fast | 'Id prayers and zakat al-Fitr.
Common mistakes: mixing the two Eids; forgetting exemptions and compensations; ignoring the social significance; saying fasting is only about hunger.

b: Name one custom for each Eid.
Give two exemptions from fasting.
State one benefit of fasting for the ummah.

activity: Make a calendar page for the Islamic year with Ramadan, 'Id al-Fitr, Dhu al-Hijjah and 'Id al-Adha. Beside each write the meaning, three customs, one symbol and one social benefit. Then write a part (c) answer plan about whether Muslims should follow traditional or modern methods to determine the start of Ramadan.

o: The meal to break the fast

check.q: What do Muslims remember on 'Id al-Adha?
Which night is believed to be better than a thousand months?

title: Islam (I5 and I6): Rites of Passage, Family, Shari'ah and Social Action
summary: Define, describe and explain birth rites, marriage, funerals, halal and haram, family teaching, the ummah, Shari'ah and its sources, zakah and sadaqah, khalifahs of the environment and Muslim charities.

sections.h: I5.1 Birth rites
p: Teach what happens and why.
• Adhan and iqamah: the father or an elder whispers the adhan into the baby's right ear and the iqamah into the left, so that the first words the baby hears are about God.
• Tahnik: rubbing something sweet, such as a chewed date, on the baby's gums, a custom of the Prophet.
• Tasmiyah: the naming. A good name is chosen, often on the seventh day.
• Head shaving and sadaqah: the baby's head is shaved and charity equal to the weight of the hair in silver or gold is given.
• Aqiqah: a sacrifice of an animal (usually one or two) with the meat shared with family and the poor. It celebrates the birth and thanks God.
• Circumcision for boys: a practice of the Prophet Ibrahim and of Muslims.
• Importance: welcoming the child into the faith community and thanking God.

b: Hearing the adhan links the baby to tawhid.
Charity shows that new life is a blessing to be shared.
Different communities do these customs in different ways and times.

sections.h: I5.2 and I5.3 Marriage and funerals
p: Marriage:
• Nikah: the Muslim marriage ceremony and legal contract (aqd nikah). Both bride and groom must agree freely. The imam usually leads it.
• Mahr: a gift (dowry) from the groom to the bride, which belongs to her.
• Witnesses: usually two witnesses attend the signing of the contract.
• Walimah: the wedding feast, which the groom hosts, often after the nikah.
• Customs before, during and after: henna, music, special clothes and prayers differ by culture.
Funerals:
• Views: the purpose of life is to worship God. Muslims believe in the sovereignty of God and akhirah, so death is a transition.

• Rituals: the shahadah is said to the dying; after death the body is washed (ghusl), wrapped in plain white cloth (kafan), funeral prayer (janazah) is said, and burial takes place as soon as possible, with the body facing Makkah.

• Mourning: for three days in general, and widows observe a longer waiting period ('iddah) of four months and ten days. Differences exist in how long families mourn and how it is shown. Reasons include culture and interpretation.

b: Some Muslim cultures hold large wedding celebrations; others very simple ones.
Mourning practices differ: some hold gatherings on the third and fortieth day; others do not.
Teachers: describe each as a custom, not as the only 'true' way.

sections.h: I5.4 and I5.5 Family life, halal and haram, tradition and change
p: The family is the basic unit of the community in Islam.

• Halal and haram: halal means permitted and haram means forbidden. For food: halal includes meat from animals slaughtered in the name of God, and haram includes pork, blood and alcohol. For clothing: modest dress; the style differs among Muslim communities.

• Roles and responsibilities of men and women: traditional teaching says men provide and protect; women care for the home and children, but women can also work and own property. Views on how this is applied vary.
• Nurture of the young and care of the elderly: parents must educate children; children must honour and care for their parents (the Qur'an, Surah 17).
• Marriage, divorce and remarriage: marriage is encouraged and divorce is allowed but discouraged. Talaq is a husband's divorce; khul' is a woman's right to initiate divorce.

• Tradition and change: some communities keep traditional roles; others support changes such as women's education and work. Social change can create emotional and spiritual challenges, for example between generations.

b: 'Traditional family roles are best for Muslim families.' Evaluate.
For: stable, follows long tradition, clear responsibilities.
Against: modern needs, women's education and work, equal partnership.
Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.

sections.h: I6.1 and I6.2 The ummah and Shari'ah
p: Define and explain the key terms.
• Ummah: the worldwide Muslim community. It gives a sense of belonging, shared responsibility and support.
• Shari'ah ('straight path'): the code of behaviour and ethics for Muslims, and a legal system. It covers worship, family life, business and conduct.
• Sources of Shari'ah: the Qur'an and the sunnah (the example and sayings of the Prophet, found in hadith).
• Fiqh ('understanding'): the study of Islamic law to understand God's law.
• Ijtihad: independent reasoning or 'intellectual struggle' by qualified scholars to give judgements on new issues.
• Ijma': agreement among qualified scholars.
• Qiyas: reasoning by analogy, comparing a new case with a similar one in the Qur'an or sunnah.
• Halal and haram: thoughts and actions that are permitted or forbidden, drawn from Shari'ah.

b: The Qur'an forbids wine (an intoxicant).
Scholars reason that other intoxicating drugs are forbidden for the same reason.
This is qiyas: using a similar reason for a new case.

sections.h: I6.3 and I6.4 Concern for others and khalifahs of the environment
p: Muslim teaching about love, compassion and concern for others.

• Zakah: obligatory charity, one of the Five Pillars. It is usually 2.5% of savings above a set amount (nisab) each year, given to the poor, those in debt and other groups named in the Qur'an. It purifies wealth.
• Sadaqah: voluntary giving of money, time, kind words or help at any time.
• What they can and cannot be used for: they can help people in need, feed the hungry, pay for education and health; they cannot be used to pay for a wealthy person's expenses or for wrongdoing.
• Wealth is loaned by God: Muslims believe wealth belongs to God and that they will be judged on how they treated others.
Khalifahs of the environment:
• Humans are khalifahs (stewards) of the Earth for God.
• God created everything and humans must care for the Earth. This can include saving water, planting trees and avoiding waste.
• The syllabus note: the focus is Muslim stewardship of the environment, not debates on treatment of animals.

b: Zakah: compulsory, fixed amount, yearly.
Sadaqah: voluntary, any amount, any time.
Both: help the poor and purify the giver's heart.

sections.h: I6.5 Muslim organisations that relieve poverty
p: Teach what each organisation does and why Muslims support it.
• Muslim Aid: an international charity that responds to poverty, disasters and education needs, motivated by Islamic teaching.
• The Red Crescent: the sister organisation of the Red Cross in many Muslim-majority countries, giving emergency relief and healthcare.
• Groups and organisations specific to a country: local charities, mosque funds, zakat committees and relief groups. Teach at least one from your students' context.
• Concern for spiritual and physical needs: many Muslim groups provide food and shelter and also education and religious guidance.
• Motivation: Qur'an teachings on charity, justice and mercy, and the example of the Prophet, who cared for the poor and orphans.

b: 'Zakah is the best way to end poverty.' Evaluate.
For: compulsory, regular, spreads wealth, supports many.
Against: needs good management; other causes of poverty need other solutions such as education and government policy.
Judgement: reasoned.

sections.h: Revision and common mistakes
p: Common mistakes.
• Mixing zakah (obligatory) and sadaqah (voluntary).
• Saying all Muslims share the same wedding or mourning customs.
• Confusing fiqh (understanding), ijtihad (independent judgement), ijma' (consensus) and qiyas (analogy).
• Saying halal only refers to food. It also includes behaviour and clothing.
Revision tasks:
• Make a four-box chart of fiqh, ijtihad, ijma' and qiyas with one example each.
• List birth, marriage and funeral rituals with their meaning.
• Write one part (b) explanation about zakah.

b: I can explain three birth rites and why they matter.
I can describe a nikah and a funeral.
I can define the four tools of fiqh.
I can name two Muslim charities and what they do.

activity: Create a 'Muslim Life Journey' timeline: birth (adhan, aqiqah), marriage (nikah, mahr, walimah), death (ghusl, janazah, burial), with one meaning for each. Add a box on zakah and sadaqah, and write a part (c) plan on whether charity is the most important duty of a Muslim.

o: A gift from the groom to the bride
A woman's right to initiate divorce
Independent judgement or intellectual struggle by qualified scholars
